paragraph.text: N8. "Who are we to interfere with nature?"

we are the same people who interfere with nature all the time, with cities, farming, medicine and environmental programmes. Helping an injured or sick animal isn't arrogance, just as helping a person isn't. And the "freedom" being protected is often just the freedom to die young of hunger or disease.
N. Wild animals, new minds and the future ·

this family takes the sentience criterion beyond exploitation. Many vegans disagree with parts of it, and the debate is legitimate. The test proposed in each chapter is simple: apply the same scenario to human beings and see whether the answer would be accepted; if it would not, that shows speciesism.
"Wild animals must be free. Who are we to decide what's good for them?"
Wild animals have a way of life of their own, independent of humans.
Respecting a being includes respecting its autonomy and way of life.
Intervening to help them replaces their way of life with our values, creates dependence and is paternalistic.
So respecting wild animals means not interfering.
P1 and P2 contain some truth. The problem lies in P3: not being hungry, cold and sick isn't a human value imposed on animals; it's what any animal seeks.
, but P3 is false in many cases.
"Wild animals must be free, not treated."
"The best thing we can do is get out of their lives."
"The sovereignty of wild animal communities must be respected."

If a little bird falls out of its nest and breaks a wing, is taking it to a vet being bossy? Of course not. It wants to fly again, and we're just helping. Respecting animals isn't leaving them to suffer. It's helping in the way they'd want, if they could ask.

We interfere with nature all the time, for ourselves: you probably live in a town or city, eat what comes from farms and take medicine when you need it. Helping a sick animal isn't arrogance, just as helping an injured person isn't. No animal wants to die of hunger or disease; helping it with that doesn't impose human values, it respects the animal's own interests.
"Is helping an unconscious person, who can't consent, arrogance or respect?"
The argument gathers several objections with the same background: the idea that helping is disrespecting.
We have no right to decide for them
We already decide, including when we do nothing
Freedom from what? From hunger and disease?

text.bold: 1. We already interfere all the time.

paragraph.text: Farming, cities, roads, dams, reforestation, reintroduction and elimination of species. We rarely call this arrogance. The charge appears almost only when the intervention aims at the good of the animals themselves.
Faced with a suffering animal we could help, omission also determines its fate. There is no neutral position.

text.bold: 3. The interests are the animals', not ours.

paragraph.text: Avoiding hunger, cold, pain and fear is what animals themselves seek. Helping them with that is taking their point of view seriously, not ours.

We help unconscious people, babies and people who can't consent without calling it paternalism, because we know they don't want to suffer. No one says vaccinating children "takes away their freedom". Denying help to animals with these arguments is applying a rule we don't apply to humans.

text.bold: 5. Respecting a way of life doesn't require accepting suffering.

paragraph.text: It's possible to respect how an animal lives and, at the same time, spare it disease, parasites and hunger. No one thinks treating a sick dog disrespects its dog nature.

text.bold: 6. Almost everyone already accepts seven kinds of intervention.

paragraph.text: Intervening to preserve species and ecosystems; to help humans, such as treating diseases or rescuing someone lost in the forest; to care for domesticated animals; to help wild animals harmed by human actions, such as oil spills; to rehabilitate wild animals and release them again; to hunt species deemed invasive, reintroduce predators, farm, build and reforest; and to vaccinate foxes against rabies in order to protect humans. If even one of these interventions is legitimate, intervening in nature isn't wrong in itself, and the question becomes why only help aimed at the animals' own good would be arrogant (Cunha, 2022, pp. 94–95).

text.bold: 7. Recognizing that someone is badly off isn't counting them for less.

paragraph.text: Saying an animal is in a worse condition, hungry or sick, isn't giving them less consideration. What would be arrogant is the opposite: thinking their suffering doesn't deserve the attention we'd give our own (Cunha, 2022, p. 94).

It's said that helping animals would impose human values. But "decided by humans" (anthropogenic) isn't the same as "serving only humans" (anthropocentric), a distinction drawn by Oscar Horta (2007). Every human decision is anthropogenic, including the decision not to help; and the rabies vaccine, decided by humans, benefits foxes. The charge, in fact, turns around: no animal venerates the species, biodiversity or balance. Those who impose foreign values on them are those who sacrifice them for these goals (Cunha, 2022, pp. 141–142).

text.bold: 9. It isn't paternalism even by Tom Regan's definition.

paragraph.text: Regan (2004), one of the main animal rights theorists, opposes intervening in nature and defines paternalism as acting for someone's good against their preference. But no animal prefers to be hungry, sick or full of parasites. When an animal flees from someone trying to help, that shows fear and lack of understanding, not a refusal of help. And the less independent someone is, the more justified it is to care for them, as we do with babies: most victims in nature are young animals (Cunha, 2022, pp. 142–143).

It's said that help would take away animals' ability to survive on their own. But a bird fed through a winter of scarcity doesn't forget how to find food; the one who loses all abilities is the one who starves. And many kinds of help create no dependence at all: vaccinating, treating a disease, or preventing the birth of young who would soon die (Cunha, 2022, pp. 146–147).

text.bold: 11. If an animal's nature makes it suffer, that's a reason to change it.

paragraph.text: Jennifer Everett (2001) and others argue that we should let each animal flourish according to its own nature. But why would the wild animal's nature be to be left to suffer, and ours to take medicine? If flourishing is what's best for the individual, helping them fulfils their nature. And if someone's nature condemns them to suffer, we treat it as we treat cancer or a genetic disease: as something to correct, not to venerate (Cunha, 2022, pp. 120–122).

text.bold: 12. "Rejecting general principles" is also a general principle.

paragraph.text: Rosalind Hursthouse (2011), a virtue ethicist, defends exploited animals but opposes intervening in nature: for her, intervention would start from a general principle, "suffering is bad", and would destroy each species' characteristic forms of life. Cunha replies that refusing general principles is itself a general principle, and that Hursthouse's conclusion also depends on one: preserving forms of life, however bad they are for those who live them (Cunha, 2022, pp. 122–123).

text.bold: 13. "There must be at least one untouched place."

paragraph.text: It's sometimes said that some place must stay free of the human hand. Ronald Dworkin (1993) distinguished two kinds of intrinsic value: incremental, where more is better, and inviolable, where it's bad for something to disappear but there's no duty to increase it. Even in the second sense, the idea doesn't explain why the human touch would make worse a situation in which someone stops suffering because they were helped. And if humans are part of nature, as is often said, human action is "natural" too (Cunha, 2022, pp. 114–119).

The seven accepted kinds of intervention, anthropocentric and anthropogenic, paternalism, dependence, flourishing according to nature, forms of life, the untouched place and sovereignty
(d) The strongest counter-reply: the sovereignty of wild communities

The most serious version comes from Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka: wild animal communities should be treated as sovereign, like peoples with a right to follow their way of life without domination. Constant interventions would make them dependent, which would be a form of colonization.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion
Donaldson and Kymlicka accept interventions in disasters and specific cases, as we would with sovereign countries. Sovereignty limits how to help; it doesn't forbid helping.
Sovereign countries receive humanitarian aid in disasters and epidemics without losing their sovereignty.
Human peoples can ask for or refuse help. Young animals starving in their first hours have no way of exercising any sovereignty.

Alasdair Cochrane (2013) and Oscar Horta (2013), along with Catia Faria (2016) and Adriano Mannino (2015), note that if sovereignty serves to protect the interests of those living in a territory, a community in which almost all members starve soon after birth looks more like a failed state than a successful sovereign people (Cunha, 2022, pp. 119–120).

text.bold: Sovereignty may call for more intervention, not less.

paragraph.text: Faria (2016) proposes "environmental improvement": any change to the environment that improves, on balance, the wellbeing of the animals living in it. If sovereignty rests on the animals' interests, it requires changing the environment when that protects them, not preserving it at any cost.

The principle being tested is: "respecting someone means not interfering in their life, even when they suffer".
Vaccinating them would be undue paternalism

It's right that respecting wild animals includes respecting their way of life, that interventions can be invasive and that creating dependence can be a problem. It's also right that humans have already done much harm to nature through careless interventions.
But respecting isn't abandoning. When helping is possible and safe, refusing help in the name of freedom or humility is letting others suffer for a principle we'd never apply to ourselves.
